title: Extracellular Fluid Balance
subject: Pathology
summary: Extracellular fluid (ECF) volume and composition are tightly regulated by sodium, water, and acid‑base mechanisms. Disruption leads to oedema, dehydration, or electrolyte disturbances that are common in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: ECF comprises plasma and interstitial fluid that bathes cells. Clinically we assess volume (hypovolaemia, euvolaemia, hypervolaemia) and composition (electrolytes, acid‑base).
b: Hypovolaemia: low blood pressure, tachycardia, dry mucous membranes.
Hypervolaemia: peripheral oedema, raised JVP, ascites.

t.a: Physical exam (BP, HR, skin turgor, JVP, peripheral oedema)
t.b: Detects volume status; low BP + tachycardia suggests hypovolaemia, raised JVP + pitting oedema suggests hypervolaemia.
Shows sodium concentration; hyponatraemia points to excess free water, hypernatraemia to water loss.
Assesses renal contribution to volume changes; high urea/creatinine with low urine output suggests renal hypovolaemia.

sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical impact and laboratory derangement.
b: Mild: asymptomatic or only mild tachycardia.
Moderate: symptomatic hypotension, oliguria, or moderate oedema.
Severe: shock, pulmonary oedema, or refractory electrolyte imbalance.

sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals the common drivers of ECF disturbance are infections, diarrhoeal disease, and limited access to safe fluids.
b: Hypovolaemia – acute diarrhoea (cholera, shigella), vomiting (malaria, gastroenteritis), haemorrhage (trauma, postpartum).
Hypervolaemia – severe malaria with capillary leak, nephrotic syndrome (post‑streptococcal), chronic heart failure (rheumatic heart disease).
Electrolyte shifts – severe burns, sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive crisis, antimalarial drug‑induced hyponatraemia.

sections.p: Patients present with signs that reflect the direction of fluid shift.
b: Hypovolaemia: orthostatic dizziness, dry tongue, sunken eyes, decreased skin turgor.
Hypervolaemia: pitting peripheral oedema, ascites, crackles in lung bases, raised JVP.
Electrolyte imbalance: muscle cramps (hypokalaemia), confusion (hypernatraemia).

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm volume status, identify the aetiology, and guide therapy.

t.b: Distinguishes renal vs extrarenal sodium loss; low urine Na (<20 mmol/L) suggests extrarenal loss (diarrhoea), high urine Na (>40 mmol/L) suggests renal loss (diuretics, renal disease).
Helps classify hyponatraemia; low osmolality with high urine Na points to SIADH, low osmolality with low urine Na points to volume depletion.
Detects IVC collapsibility (hypovolaemia) or pleural effusion/pulmonary oedema (hypervolaemia). If unavailable, rely on clinical signs.

sections.p: Uncorrected ECF derangements can rapidly become fatal.
b: Severe hypovolaemia → shock, acute kidney injury, myocardial ischaemia.
Severe hypervolaemia → pulmonary oedema, respiratory failure, hepatic congestion.
Rapid electrolyte shifts → cardiac arrhythmias, seizures.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then correct volume and electrolyte abnormalities.
b: Hypovolaemia: isotonic saline bolus 20 mL/kg (if IV access possible); oral rehydration solution (ORS) for mild cases.
Hypervolaemia: restrict sodium intake, give loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) unless contraindicated by severe dehydration.
Hyponatraemia: give hypertonic saline only if neurological symptoms; otherwise limit free water.
Hypernatraemia: give gradual hypotonic fluids (5 % dextrose) to avoid cerebral oedema.

sections.p: Re‑assess volume status after each intervention and educate on safe fluid practices.
b: Daily weight and input‑output chart for chronic heart failure or renal disease.
Teach ORS preparation for diarrhoeal illnesses.
Screen for underlying chronic disease (e.g., HIV, TB) that predisposes to fluid shifts.
Dehydration vs. diabetes insipidus – both cause polyuria, but DI has low urine osmolality despite normal volume.
Pulmonary oedema vs. severe pneumonia – both cause crackles; oedema improves with diuretics, pneumonia with antibiotics.

sections.p: Lab values may be deceptive in certain settings.
b: Serum sodium may appear normal in mixed hypo‑ and hyper‑natremia; interpret with clinical picture.
Urine sodium can be falsely low in patients on recent diuretics; ask medication history.

whenToSeekHelp: Unresponsive patient with suspected severe hyponatraemia or hypernatraemia
Shock unresponsive to initial fluid bolus
Rapidly worsening pulmonary oedema causing respiratory distress

faq.q: Why does sodium drive extracellular fluid volume?
faq.a: Sodium determines plasma osmolality; water follows sodium, so retaining sodium expands ECF.

faq.q: Can a patient be both dehydrated and have peripheral oedema?
faq.a: Yes, in conditions like severe protein loss (nephrotic syndrome) where intravascular volume is low but interstitial fluid accumulates.

faq.q: What is the first bedside step in a patient with suspected hypovolaemia?
faq.a: Assess orthostatic vitals and skin turgor; start isotonic fluid bolus if shock is evident.

exam: A 6‑year‑old with severe diarrhoea presents with sunken eyes and a capillary refill >3 seconds — discuss immediate management and how you would confirm hypovolaemia without labs.
A patient with known rheumatic heart disease develops sudden breathlessness and bilateral crackles — differentiate pulmonary oedema from pneumonia and outline the first therapeutic action.
In a malaria patient you note a rising JVP and pitting oedema of the ankles — explain the pathophysiology of capillary leak and list two investigations you would order if ultrasound is unavailable.

A postpartum woman presents with hypotension, tachycardia, and a large abdominal girth — what are the key causes of extracellular fluid expansion in this setting and how would you prioritize treatment?
A patient on chronic diuretics shows hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality — what question would you ask to distinguish SIADH from volume depletion?

You receive a lab report showing normal serum sodium but the patient has marked peripheral oedema — what potential laboratory pitfall should you consider and what bedside test can clarify the picture?
